parts.text:
26 Monochromatic light of wavelength 5.30 × 10–7
m is incident normally on a diffraction grating. The
first order maximum is observed at an angle of 15.4° to the direction of the incident light.
What is the angle between the first and second order diffraction maxima?
A
7.7°
B
15.4°
C
16.7°
D
32.1°

hints: Notice the given $\lambda = 5.30 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ and first order $\theta_1 = 15.4^{\circ}$ for normal incidence on the grating.
Connect the orders with $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$, so $\sin\theta_2 = 2\sin\theta_1$ and the grating spacing $d$ cancels.
Calculate $\theta_2$ from $2\sin 15.4^{\circ}$, then subtract $15.4^{\circ}$ to get the separation between the two maxima.
walkthrough: Write the grating equation for normal incidence: $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$, with $n=1$ for first order and $n=2$ for second order.
The required separation is $\theta_2 - \theta_1 \approx 32.1^{\circ} - 15.4^{\circ} = 16.7^{\circ}$. This is option C.

A.explanation: Halving $15.4^{\circ}$ has no physical basis because $\sin\theta$ is proportional to $n$, not $\theta$ itself.

B.explanation: The maxima are not equally spaced in angle because $\theta = \sin^{-1}(n\lambda/d)$ is non-linear in $n$.

C.explanation: Second order is at about $32.1^{\circ}$ from the centre, so the separation from $15.4^{\circ}$ is about $16.7^{\circ}$.

D.explanation: About $32.1^{\circ}$ is the angle of the second order from the incident direction, not the angle between first and second order.
